UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE  
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms 
) 
) 
Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
 
COMMENTS  
BY 
OFFICE OF THE OHIO CONSUMERS’ COUNSEL 
 
 
I.  
INTRODUCTION 
The Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel (“OCC”), on behalf of Ohio’s residential 
utility consumers, respectfully submits these comments regarding reforms to the governance of 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”). 
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or “Commission”) examination 
of PJM governance is both timely and necessary. Under the Federal Power Act, FERC is 
responsible for protecting consumers from rates, terms, and conditions of wholesale electric 
service that are unjust and unreasonable. Yet the institutional structure through which PJM 
develops the rules governing wholesale markets, resource adequacy, and transmission planning 
gives the consumers who ultimately pay those costs remarkably little leverage in the processes 
and decisions that produce them. That is problematic on many fronts.  
That imbalance matters. PJM serves approximately 67 million consumers across 14 
jurisdictions. But those consumers are represented in the PJM stakeholder process by only 14 
statutory consumer advocate votes—one for each jurisdiction. At the Standing Committee and 
Senior Task Force level, those consumer advocates constitute approximately 1.3 percent of 
potential voters. Even at the Markets and Reliability Committee (“MRC”) and Members

2 
Committee (“MC”), where sector-weighted voting applies, consumer advocates account for only 
a small portion of the voting influence. 
Meanwhile, entities with direct financial interests in PJM market rules and transmission 
decisions comprise much of PJM’s membership and exercise substantial influence over the 
development of those rules. The result is a fundamental structural problem: many of the entities 
voting on proposals governing wholesale electricity markets and transmission investment have a 
financial interest in the revenues those rules produce. At the same time, residential consumers 
who ultimately pay the resulting charges, have comparatively little ability to shape those 
proposals. 
FERC should address that imbalance as a central component of PJM governance reform. 
But there is more to be done.  
Governance reform should not merely redistribute authority among PJM’s existing 
institutional actors. It should make PJM more accountable to the public that it serves. That 
requires, at minimum, making affordability and the public interest an express component of 
PJM’s responsibilities, implementing consumer safeguards for transmission planning, 
strengthening the voices of statutory consumer advocates, improving transparency and cost 
oversight, and ensuring that any expansion of the PJM Board’s authority is accompanied by 
meaningful safeguards protecting consumers. 
OCC’s responses to the Commission’s specific list of questions attached to the Notice 
Requesting Post-Conference Comment issued in this docket on July 30, 2026, are appended as 
Attachment A to these comments.

3 
II.  
REFORMS TO PJM GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE 
A. 
PJM governance must expressly recognize affordability and the public 
interest. 
PJM performs functions that profoundly affect the affordability and reliability of 
electricity service for over 67 million Americans. Its capacity market, energy markets, and 
transmission planning processes produce billions of dollars in costs that ultimately flow through 
to consumers’ electric bills. These electric transmission and supply charges comprise 60 to 70% 
of an Ohio household’s electricity bill, all pass-through charges from FERC and PJM.1  
Yet affordability is not embedded in PJM’s governance structure. Unlike reliability – 
which PJM expressly calls its “primary responsibility,” – affordability is not treated as a 
comparable institutional obligation. PJM instead points to the states to address the retail impact 
of rising wholesale costs.2 
Reliability is indispensable. But reliability cannot mean reliability at any cost. The 
Federal Power Act’s consumer-protection mandate requires rates to be “just and reasonable.” 
Energy markets and transmission planning should produce reliable service efficiently and at 
reasonable cost. 
PJM’s governing documents should expressly require PJM and its Board to act in the 
public interest and to consider affordability alongside reliability. This should be a substantive 
obligation, not an aspirational statement. PJM should be required to evaluate the consumer cost 
consequences of material proposals and major Board decisions. A governance structure that 
measures reliability consequences but does not meaningfully measure and consider consumer 
 
1 Public Utilities Commission of Ohio, Ohio Utility Rate Survey (June 2026).  
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket Nos. EL 25-49-000 and -001, Informational Report, Exhibit A at 2 (Jan. 20, 
2026) (“PJM must be conscious of the affordability challenges facing the 67 million consumers in our footprint 
today. There is much that our states can be doing to contend with the higher wholesale costs at the retail level.”) 
(citation omitted).

4 
cost consequences falls far short of providing just and reasonable rates for consumers. 
Affordability should accordingly become an institutional responsibility against which PJM’s 
performance can be measured. 
B. 
Independent cost oversight on transmission projects is needed. 
Transmission deserves particular attention in the form of an Independent Transmission 
Monitor. Transmission charges can account for up to 20% of an Ohio household’s electricity 
bill.3 
PJM consumers face substantial and growing transmission costs. From 2017 through 
2025, Ohio transmission project costs have ballooned with over $16.4 billion in costs, with 
supplemental projects accounting for 66% of those projects, $10.8 billion. 4 These huge 
transmission bills to Ohio consumers emanate from massive transmission investment and the 
cost allocation methodologies used to collect that investment in regional and supplemental 
transmission projects.  
Ohio consumers’ experience with supplemental transmission projects demonstrates the 
need for independent transmission oversight. Under PJM’s existing framework, supplemental 
projects are not subject to PJM review for need, prudence or cost-effectiveness. Yet the costs are 
recovered from consumers through FERC-jurisdictional transmission rates.  
In Ohio, no one is filling that gap by reviewing these projects for prudence, need, or cost-
effectiveness before consumers are required to pay for them. OCC’s 2023 complaint to FERC 
highlighted the magnitude of the problem: based on data through 2022 available at the time of 
that filing, Ohio utilities had added to local transmission infrastructures over approximately six 
 
3 PUCO, Ohio Utility Rate Survey (June 2026).  
4 Sourced from PJM State of Ohio Infrastructure Reports 2017-2025.

5 
years nearly $6 billion in supplemental project costs that were not reviewed by any regulatory 
authority for need, prudence or cost-effectiveness. This problem keeps growing. Supplemental 
Projects continue to make up the bulk of annual investment in transmission infrastructure. 
This regulatory gap creates precisely the wrong incentive – utilities can pursue substantial 
transmission investment without the meaningful, independent scrutiny that should precede the 
imposition of monopoly costs on captive consumers. The persistence of that gap also 
demonstrates why governance reform cannot rely on existing institutions to correct themselves. 
OCC filed its complaint in September 2023 asking FERC to remedy the lack of regulatory 
oversight and requested expedited treatment because additional projects and costs would 
continue accumulating while the complaint remained unresolved. True to form, subsequent 
supplemental transmission spending has continued to increase. From 2023 to 2025, an additional 
$4.3 billion has been spent on Ohio supplemental transmission projects, bringing the total since 
2017 to over $10 billion. Nearly three years after filing the complaint, FERC still has not ruled 
on OCC’s Complaint. Docket No. EL23-105-000 remains on the Commission’s list of pending 
complaints. 
Yet there is no transmission equivalent of PJM’s Independent Market Monitor providing 
comprehensive, independent scrutiny of transmission planning incentives, costs, and outcomes. 
That gap is especially troubling for transmission projects receiving limited regional scrutiny, 
including transmission-owner Supplemental Projects that are proliferating in Ohio.  
The existing structure can create incentives favoring locally planned, cost-of-service 
transmission investment over regional solutions that may provide broader benefits or greater 
efficiency. Consumers ultimately bear the consequences of those incentives through their electric 
bills.

6 
An independent transmission monitor would help close this accountability gap by 
providing ongoing, independent scrutiny of the need, alternatives and costs associated with 
transmission investment – including Supplemental Projects. This would replace the current 
process where consumers must rely on after-the-fact challenges to formula transmission rates 
while billions of dollars in costs continue to be incurred. An independent transmission monitor 
should be structurally independent from PJM and transmission owners and should have sufficient 
access to information to conduct meaningful analysis. 
Independent oversight would not replace PJM’s planning responsibilities, existing state 
oversight authority or the Commission’s jurisdiction. It would provide FERC, states, consumer 
advocates, and stakeholders with an independent source of information needed to determine 
whether billions of dollars in transmission investment are prudent, efficient, and beneficial to 
consumers. 
C. 
Enhancing the PJM Attachment M-3 Supplemental Project process. 
The growth in AI load interconnection requests is driving the need for improved local and 
Supplemental Project transmission planning processes. Although the Supplemental Projects are 
not directly governed by the requirements of FERC Order No. 1920, the Commission’s recent 
actions reflect an increasing emphasis on transparent planning processes, meaningful stakeholder 
participation, cost-effective analyses, and well-supported planning records. Those essential 
elements are lacking in the present PJM process.  
In Order No. 1920, the Commission concluded that more forward-looking and 
transparent transmission planning is necessary to ensure that transmission investments remain 
just and reasonable over the long term. While that rule principally addresses long-term regional 
transmission planning, the policy objectives it advances – including transparency, robust

7 
planning assumptions, and meaningful stakeholder engagement—are equally relevant to 
customer-driven supplemental transmission projects.  
Importantly, Order No. 8905 required similar transparency, robust planning assumptions 
and meaningful stakeholder engagement in the local transmission planning process. In PJM, 
Supplemental Projects are part of the local planning process and must be planned in a manner 
that encompasses these principles. 
The PJM Attachment M-3 planning process for local transmission projects and 
Supplemental Projects embrace some, but not all these principles. OCC recognizes that FERC 
accepted the current PJM Attachment M-3 local transmission planning process in 2020 but notes 
that FERC has more recently questioned whether that process is sufficient in its April 2022 
Supplemental Notice of Technical Conference in Docket No. AD22-8-000. That Notice states: 
The purpose of this conference is to explore measures to ensure 
sufficient transparency into and cost effectiveness of local and 
regional transmission planning decisions, including: (1) the role of 
cost management measures in ensuring the cost-effective 
identification of local transmission needs (e.g., planning criteria) 
and solutions to address identified local transmission and regional 
reliability-related transmission needs; and (2) cost considerations 
and the processes through which transmission developers recover 
their costs to ensure just and reasonable transmission rates.6 
 
Although FERC did not require changes to the local and Supplemental Project transmission 
planning process in Order No. 1920, it clearly left the door open for improvements in that 
process.  
 
5 Preventing Undue Discrimination and Preference in Transmission Service, Order No. 890, 118 FERC ¶ 61,119 at 
P 3, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,241 (2007) (“Order No. 890”), order on reh’g, Order No. 890-A, 121 FERC ¶ 
61,297, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,261 (2007) (“Order No. 890-A”); order on reh’g, Order No. 890-B, 123 FERC ¶ 
61,299 (2008); order on reh’g, Order No. 890-C, 126 FERC ¶ 61,228 (2009). 
6 Transmission Planning and Cost Management, Docket No. AD22-8-000, Supplemental Notice of Technical 
Conference at 1, (July 22, 2022).

8 
In a move toward creating greater transparency around that process, FERC recently 
issued show-cause orders directing several public utility transmission providers, including PJM 
in Docket No. EL26-67-000, to explain why aspects of their local and Supplemental Project 
transmission planning processes remain just and reasonable under the Federal Power Act. These 
proceedings reflect FERC’s movement toward a broader regulatory focus on transparency, 
justification, cost-effectiveness and oversight of local and Supplemental Project transmission 
investments.  
These show cause proceedings reinforce the importance of ensuring that local and 
Supplemental transmission projects are supported by demonstrated need, prudent engineering, 
transparent planning assumptions, project cost-effectiveness and a planning record sufficient to 
permit meaningful stakeholder review before significant investments are undertaken. These 
elements are missing from the current PJM Attachment M-3 planning process.  
Customer-driven project presentations to the Sub-regional RTEP committee and the 
TEAC committee should include additional information regarding the basis for projected load 
growth. Without disclosing confidential commercial information, transmission owners should 
identify the extent to which projected customer demand is supported by executed service 
agreements, meaningful development milestones, or other objective indicators demonstrating the 
likelihood that the projected load will materialize.  
Transmission owners should be more fully discussing alternatives considered during 
project development. For projects presented at the Solutions stage, stakeholders should 
understand not only the preferred solution but also the principle alternatives evaluated, the 
reasons those alternatives were not selected, and whether phased implementation, equipment 
upgrades, operational changes, or other lower-cost options were considered.

9 
Transmission owners should also address substantive stakeholder comments as projects 
advance through subsequent stages of the M-3 process. OCC is not suggesting that transmission 
owners be required to provide formal written responses to every comment. However, a brief 
discussion during subsequent TEAC presentations explaining whether significant stakeholder 
concerns were considered and, where appropriate, how they were addressed, would strengthen 
the planning record and improve stakeholder confidence in the process.  
PJM and transmission owners should at a minimum provide information requested by 
stakeholders during these processes about specific planned projects. To date, despite several 
requests by OCC for information as part of the July and August Attachment M-3 stakeholder 
processes in PJM, PJM and the Ohio transmission Owners still have not provided substantive 
responses to OCC’s requests for information regarding specific projects.7 Those questions seek 
information related to the planning assumptions, alternatives considered and cost-efficiency of 
certain identified proposed Supplemental Projects in Ohio. 
Finally, OCC encourages continued dialogue among PJM, transmission owners, states, 
consumer advocates, and other stakeholders regarding the evolution of Supplemental Project 
transmission planning, especially where those local transmission projects may be related to large 
load and Artificial Intelligence data centers. This customer-driven transmission investment 
represents a significant and growing component of transmission development throughout the 
PJM region, both in the Regional Transmission Expansion Planning process and in the 
Attachment M-3 Supplemental Project planning process. As planning practices continue to 
evolve, regular stakeholder discussions regarding transparency, planning assumptions, customer 
commitments, and cost responsibility will help ensure that the M-3 process provides meaningful 
 
7 See Attachment B.

10 
opportunities for stakeholder participation while supporting timely, reliable, and cost-effective 
transmission planning. 
D. 
Transparency for PJM meetings. 
Transparency in PJM meetings and decision-making is essential. PJM makes decisions 
that have enormous consequences for the over 67 million consumers who pay electric bills. 
Decisions affecting capacity and energy costs, transmission investment, market rules, and 
reliability should not be developed through closed-door discussions or processes that leave 
consumers and their representatives unable to understand who advocated for outcomes and why. 
Open meetings, accessible materials, meaningful opportunity for public and consumer 
participation, and a clear record of the basis for PJM’s decisions would promote accountability 
and public confidence. It would also help ensure that consumer affordability and broader public 
interest receive meaningful consideration alongside the interests of PJM’s market participants. 
The Board’s deliberations and decision-making should, whenever practicable, occur in meetings 
open to stakeholders and the public, with limited exceptions only where confidentiality is legally 
or commercially required. 
III. 
STATE PARTICIPATION  
State participation must be formalized- but state representation cannot substitute for 
consumer representation. 
PJM governance reform should substantially strengthen the role of the states and the role 
of consumer advocates. FERC should recognize an important distinction: strengthening the “state 
voice” is not synonymous with strengthening the consumer voice. 
State utility commissions, governors, legislators, environmental agencies, economic-
development officials, and statutory consumer advocates perform different functions. State 
commissions may balance reliability, utility financial integrity, economic development,

11 
environmental requirements, and other statutory considerations. Governors and legislatures 
likewise balance numerous competing public-policy objectives. Statutory consumer advocates 
have a different responsibility: protecting utility consumers, including residential consumers, 
from excessive, unjust and unreasonable utility costs. 
Those unique consumer interests often overlap with the states’ interests, but they are not 
identical. Consumer advocates may agree with their state commissions on one issue and disagree 
on another. PJM governance reform should preserve those independent perspectives rather than 
subsuming consumer representation within a generalized category of “state interests.” 
Accordingly, FERC should strengthen the role of both representative voices in the processes. 
OPSI should receive meaningful jump-ball filing rights where a sufficiently broad 
consensus of states supports an alternative to a PJM proposal. While the Commission has 
provided for such filing rights in the context of cost allocation proposals for long-term regional 
transmission projects in Order No. 1920, no similar rights exist for the Order No. 1000 and Order 
No. 890 regional and local transmission planning processes. PJM should also be required to 
consult formally with OPSI before any major section 205 filings, including significant resource-
adequacy and transmission planning and cost allocation filings. At the same time, statutory 
consumer advocates should retain an independent and meaningful role throughout PJM 
governance, including in the stakeholder process and in the selection of PJM Board members. 
 
IV.  
STAKEHOLDER PROCESS 
A. 
Consumers need meaningful cost information before PJM makes decisions. 
PJM cannot credibly claim that its processes produce cost-effective outcomes if neither 
decision-makers nor stakeholders are routinely provided with information about what the

12 
proposals will cost consumers. Cost analysis should become an ordinary part of PJM governance 
– a part that is freely and timely shared with interested parties, including consumer advocates. 
For material proposals advancing to the MRC or MC, PJM should provide a reasonable 
assessment of expected cost impacts sufficiently early for stakeholders to use that information in 
evaluating competing proposals. The analysis need not – and often cannot – predict costs with 
precision. But uncertainty is not a justification for providing no analysis. 
PJM routinely analyzes complicated questions involving reliability, resource adequacy, 
market behavior, and system conditions under uncertain future assumptions. Consumer cost 
consequences deserve comparable institutional attention. 
Cost information would improve not only consumer protection but decision-making 
itself. Stakeholders could evaluate whether incremental reliability benefits justify incremental 
costs, compare alternatives on a more informed basis, and identify proposals that accomplish the 
same objective at lower consumer cost. 
FERC should require PJM to institutionalize meaningful and transparent cost-impact 
analysis. FERC also should require PJM and the transmission owners to provide answers to 
specific questions from stakeholders, including consumers advocates, about identified projects 
during the stakeholder process. Such questions include information regarding cost analyses, 
planning assumptions, alternatives considered and other cost impact data. There should be 
consequences for PJM’s and/or the transmission owners’ failure to respond to such specific 
questions about identified projects. In the absence of any realistic process for challenging the 
prudence, need for and cost-efficiency of local or Supplemental Projects in the formula 
transmission rate challenge process, consumers must have access to information regarding these 
projects during the transmission planning stage before construction begins.

13 
B. 
Stakeholder voting should prevent affiliate voting from overwhelming 
consumer interests. 
PJM’s stakeholder process should facilitate genuine consensus rather than allow entities 
with numerous affiliates to dominate the early stages of policy development. Ohio illustrates how 
PJM’s affiliate-voting rules dilute the consumer voice at the committees where proposals are 
developed.  
OCC, the statutory representative of 4.5 million residential households, receives one vote 
to represent Ohio’s residential utility consumers. Utilities participate through corporate families 
with numerous PJM affiliates. For example, Ohio Power Company is part of the AEP corporate 
family, which includes multiple transmission, generation, and energy affiliates. Ohio Edison is 
part of the FirstEnergy corporate family. Duke Energy Ohio participates alongside other Duke 
affiliates. At Standing Committees and Senior Task Forces, where affiliate voting is permitted, 
these corporate families can potentially exercise many multiple votes while OCC has one.  
That distinction is particularly important because the detailed work of designing PJM 
rules often occurs at Standing Committees and Senior Task Forces before proposals reach the 
Markets and Reliability Committee (MRC) or the Members Committee (MC). While the MRC 
and MC may be governed by weighted sector voting requirements, the same is not true of the 
other Standing Committees and Task Forces. This can permit supply-side or other commercial 
interests to advance proposals without meaningful support from those who represent the 
consumers responsible for paying the resulting costs. That is fundamentally unfair.  
By the time proposals reach sector-weighted voting at the MRC and MC, it may be too 
late for consumer interests to meaningfully shape their design. Those interests may instead be 
left primarily with the ability to vote no on a proposal developed without their meaningful 
participation.

14 
FERC should encourage PJM to address this structural problem by extending sector-
weighted voting, or comparable protections against affiliate-vote dominance, to Standing 
Committees and Senior Task Forces. Doing so would not silence any sector but rather would 
levelize the playing field for all stakeholder interests. It would encourage those submitting 
proposals to attract support across sectors earlier in the development process, when compromise 
can meaningfully affect their substance. 
C. 
PJM voting should be transparent. 
PJM should also disclose how individual member companies vote throughout the 
stakeholder process. Entities participating in PJM are voting on matters that affect more than 
their private commercial interests. They participate in developing rules affecting the reliability 
and cost of electricity service for approximately 67 million consumers. 
Aggregate voting results provide insufficient accountability and can impede consensus-
building. When a proposal narrowly fails, stakeholders should be able to identify the concerns 
preventing agreement and determine whether modifications could produce broader support. 
Transparency would also eliminate inconsistent disclosure obligations. Some utilities 
may already be required under state law to disclose PJM votes, while others are not. In contrast, 
public consumer advocates operate under public-records requirements. PJM-wide disclosure 
would establish a uniform standard that could easily be followed. Individual member votes 
should be publicly available at all material levels of the stakeholder process. 
V.  
PJM BOARD INDEPENDENCE 
 
PJM Board reform should increase public accountability while preserving board 
independence. 
Any expansion of Board authority should be accompanied by greater Board 
accountability.

15 
First, the Board’s required expertise should include meaningful experience with state 
regulation and consumer interests. PJM should include Board members who understand how 
wholesale market and transmission decisions ultimately appear on consumers’ retail electric 
bills. 
Second, the process for selecting Board members should include greater state and 
consumer participation. The Nominating Committee should include representation designated by 
states as well as a statutory consumer advocate. Consumers should not depend upon occasional 
rotation within the End-Use Customer Sector for representation in selecting the individuals who 
ultimately exercise enormous authority over costs paid by those consumers. 
Third, Board decision-making should be substantially more transparent. Board votes on 
significant matters should be disclosed, and the Board should provide meaningful explanations 
for consequential decisions. Appropriate portions of Board meetings should also be open or 
otherwise made available to stakeholders and the public. 
Transparency should not, however, come at the expense of independence. FERC should 
not relax appropriate restrictions on private communication between individual Board members 
and interested market participants. Greater transparency in Board deliberations provides a better 
means of increasing accountability than expanding private access. 
 
VI. 
SECTION 205 FILING RIGHTS 
FERC should not expand the PJM Board’s Section 205 authority without corresponding 
consumer and state safeguards. 
The Commission should proceed cautiously before expanding or limiting the PJM 
Board’s unilateral filing authority under section 205 of the Federal Power Act. The relevant 
question is not simply whether other RTO boards possess broader section 205 authority. The 
question is whether expanding or limiting authority to PJM’s Board, under PJM’s existing

16 
governance structure, would produce decision-making that better protects consumers and results 
in just and reasonable rates. 
 
More importantly the Commission has already spoken on the concept of limiting the 
Board’s existing filing rights related to transmission planning. In Docket Nos. ER24-2336, 
ER24-2338 and EL24-119, the Commission rejected efforts by the Transmission Owners to 
provide themselves with extensive, unilateral veto rights with respect to the transmission 
planning process. In those cases, PJM and the Transmission Owners proposed to move the 
planning process rules from the PJM Operating Agreement to the PJM Open Access 
Transmission Tariff and the Consolidated Transmission Owners’ Agreement. FERC found that 
such action would provide the Transmission Owners with undue influence over the transmission 
planning process.8 The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the Commission’s rulings just 
two months ago.9 There is no reason to revisit these very recent decisions.  
At a minimum, PJM’s governing documents should first be revised to establish 
affordability and the public interest as express Board responsibilities. States and consumer 
advocates should also receive meaningful “jump ball” filing rights that allow a sufficiently broad 
consensus to present an alternative proposal to the Commission. 
Providing FERC with competing proposals would not displace the Commission’s 
ultimate responsibility to determine what is just and reasonable. Instead, it would ensure that the 
Commission hears a meaningful alternative from governmental entities responsible for protecting 
consumer interests. 
 
8 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,181(2024), order denying reh’g, 192 FERC ¶ 61,051 (2025). 
9 PJM Transmission Owners v. FERC, No. 25-1064 (D.C. Cir. June 5, 2026) (per curiam).

17 
VII.  CONCLUSION 
The Commission should evaluate PJM governance reform from the perspective of the 
consumers whom the Federal Power Act ultimately protects. The fundamental problem is not 
simply whether authority resides with PJM’s Members Committee, its Board, or another 
institutional actor. The problem is whether PJM’s governance structure produces transparent, 
accountable, cost-conscious decisions consistent with just and reasonable rates. At the present 
time, PJM’s governance structure is not doing the job.  
The reforms discussed in these OCC comments would not guarantee that every PJM 
decision produces the outcome preferred by consumers, states, market participants, or any other 
constituency. The reforms would, however, make it substantially more likely that decisions 
affecting tens of millions of consumers are made through a process that gives weight to 
affordability, provides meaningful public accountability, and supplies the Commission with the 
information and competing perspectives necessary to fulfill its responsibility under the Federal 
Power Act to protect consumers from unjust and unreasonable rates.

18 
Respectfully submitted,

Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel Response to Commission Questions in Notice 
Requesting Post-Conference Comments 
PJM Board Independence 
Questions/Comments 
Yes 
No 
1) 
Should Board members’ terms be extended to five or more years? 
X 
Comments: Longer terms for Board members could help ensure a more knowledgeable 
Board with a longer-term perspective that is less susceptible to stakeholder pressure. 
However, terms should not be too long to reduce accountability to Members (including 
consumer advocates) and make it more difficult to influence the Board when change is 
needed. 
2) 
Should there be a maximum number of years that a Board member may 
serve (e.g., 10 years)? 
X 
Comments: While a longer term may promote Board independence and allow members 
to develop greater institutional knowledge, a single term greater than five years without 
the possibility of reelection would likely reduce accountability to Members and make 
the Board too insulated from Member feedback. Some opportunity for periodic 
reevaluation of Board performance better balances independence with accountability. 
Periodic refreshment in the board is a benefit.  
3) 
Should the Board member qualification rules be revised to provide a 
preference for some Board members that reside in the PJM region? 
X 
Comments: While Board members must act in the interests of the PJM region as a 
whole, residing within the region helps ensure they remain connected to the 
affordability and reliability concerns experienced by the consumers ultimately served by 
PJM. Regional familiarity strengthens understanding of consumer impacts and state 
policy. 
4) 
Should the conflict-of-interest rules be revised to reduce the cooling off 
period for Board members from two years to one year? 
X 
Comments: The two-year cooling-off period helps preserve the Board’s independence 
by reducing conflicts of interest arising from recent employment with PJM Members. A 
cooling off period is required in Ohio when it comes to both the state consumer 
advocate and the PUCO commissioners.  
5) 
Should restrictions on Board communications be relaxed to enable more 
communication between the Board and stakeholders? 
X

Comments: FERC should not relax appropriate restrictions on private communications 
between individual Board members and interested market participants. Greater 
transparency in Board deliberations provides a better means of increasing accountability

6) 
In order to increase transparency, should Board votes be made public or the 
Board be required to explain its reasoning?  
X 
 
 
Comments: To promote transparency, Board votes on significant matters should be 
disclosed, and the Board should provide meaningful explanations for consequential 
decisions.  
7) 
In order to increase transparency, should some Board meetings be open or 
available to the public? 
X 
 
 
Comments: Appropriate portions of Board meetings should be open or otherwise made 
available to stakeholders and the public. The Board’s deliberations and decision-making 
should, whenever practicable, occur in meetings that are open to stakeholders and the 
public, with limited exceptions only where confidentiality is legally or commercially 
required. 
8) 
Should PJM’s governing documents be revised to explicitly state that the 
responsibility of PJM and its Board is to serve the public interest? 
X 
 
 
Comments: PJM should expressly recognize in governing documents its obligation to 
serve the public interest and consider affordability as well as reliability of service for 
consumers in the region.  
9) 
Should state representatives have at least one voting member on the 
Nominating Committee? 
X 
 
 
Comments: States should have representation on the Nominating Committee. It 
promotes balanced governance and broader public accountability.  
10) 
Should PJM adopt public performance metrics and tie management 
compensation to their achievement? 
 
X 
 
Comments: Tying PJM management compensation to achievement and public 
performance metrics could result in PJM management focusing on reliability at all costs 
to the detriment of consumers who must pay high rates for transmission service. Energy 
markets and transmission planning should produce reliable service efficiently and at 
reasonable cost.

I.
Introduction
The Ohio Office of the Consumers' Counsel (OCC) appreciates the opportunity to submit these 
Comments and Information Requests regarding the supplemental transmission projects presented by 
American Electric Power (AEP), FirstEnergy ATSI (ATSI), Duke Energy Ohio (DEOK), and AES 
Ohio (AES) at the July 7, 2026, meeting of the PJM Transmission Expansion Advisory Committee 
(TEAC). 
OCC submits these comments in support of the purposes of PJM's M-3 Supplemental Project 
Process. As reflected in PJM Manual 14B, the Regional Transmission Expansion Planning Process 
is intended to promote transparency, facilitate meaningful stakeholder participation, and improve 
transmission planning through the early identification and evaluation of planning assumptions, 
transmission needs, proposed solutions, and local transmission plans. Transparency during the M-3 
process benefits transmission owners, PJM, regulators, and consumers by promoting informed 
discussion regarding planning assumptions, project need, alternatives, and anticipated consumer 
impact. OCC’s comments are intended to further these objectives by requesting information 
necessary for stakeholders to meaningfully evaluate customer-driven supplemental transmission 
projects.   
OCC supports prudent transmission investment necessary to maintain a reliable and resilient 
transmission system. At the same time, transmission investments are long-lived assets whose costs 
ultimately may be borne by consumers. Accordingly, transmission planning should remain 
transparent, data-driven, and consistent with the principle that costs should follow cost causation.  
These Comments and Information Requests are consistent with OCC's longstanding interest in 
ensuring that supplemental transmission projects are supported by transparent planning 
assumptions, demonstrated need, prudent engineering, and appropriate consumer protections. 
Nothing in these comments is intended to address the merits of any pending regulatory proceeding. 
Rather, OCC seeks to ensure that the project-specific record developed through the M-3 process is 
as complete and transparent as possible.

1.  
The Need for Standardized Reporting  
OCC encourages PJM and transmission owners to provide standardized reporting identifying: (1) 
projected load attributable to native load, ordinary growth, and large-load customers; (2) whether 
customer load is supported by executed service agreements or other binding commitments; (3) 
customer development milestones; (4) anticipated in-service schedules; (5) sensitivity analyses for 
delayed or cancelled projects; and (6) whether facilities can be phased as customer commitments 
mature. 
 
2.   
The Need for Transparency  
Customer-driven supplemental transmission projects differ in important respects from traditional 
reliability-driven transmission projects. Historically, many supplemental projects were developed to 
address aging infrastructure, equipment replacement, operational flexibility, or identified reliability 
violations based on existing system conditions. By contrast, customer-driven projects are often 
initiated in anticipation of substantial future load growth associated with one or more specific 
customers seeking new or expanded electric service. As a result, these projects frequently depend 
upon assumptions regarding the timing, magnitude, and certainty of future customer demand rather 
than existing system deficiencies. That distinction makes transparency regarding planning 
assumptions, customer commitments, forecast certainty, and project timing particularly important. 
Without sufficient information regarding those underlying assumptions, stakeholders cannot 
meaningfully evaluate whether the proposed transmission investment is appropriately timed, 
appropriately sized, or reasonably necessary to serve the anticipated customer load. 
The projects presented at the July 7, 2026 TEAC meeting illustrate this distinction. Three of the 
four Ohio projects were driven primarily by anticipated customer load growth, while one addressed 
an operational limitation on the existing transmission system. OCC's comments reflect those 
differences by applying a common set of planning principles while recognizing that the information 
necessary to evaluate customer-driven projects is not identical to that required for traditional 
reliability or operational projects. 
3. 
The Value of Phased in Construction in Customer-Driven Transmission Planning  
As customer-driven supplemental transmission projects continue to increase in size and complexity, 
transmission owners should, where practical, evaluate whether proposed facilities can be developed 
in phases that correspond with demonstrated customer demand. Phased implementation is a well-
established planning approach that allows infrastructure to be expanded as customer development 
progresses while maintaining the flexibility necessary to provide reliable electric service.

For projects driven by anticipated future load growth, phased construction may reduce the risk of 
premature investment if projected customer demand is delayed, reduced, or ultimately does not 
materialize. Rather than requiring the construction of facilities sized for the maximum projected 
load at the outset, phased implementation can allow transmission owners to provide service as 
customer commitments become more certain and system needs evolve. This approach can reduce 
the likelihood that consumers will bear the costs of transmission facilities that exceed what is 
reasonably necessary to serve actual demand. 
Accordingly, OCC encourages transmission owners to discuss, as part of the M-3 process, whether 
phased implementation was considered during project development, the engineering and economic 
factors supporting the selected approach, and how the proposed construction schedule aligns with 
anticipated customer development. Providing this information will improve transparency, 
strengthen the planning record, and enhance stakeholder confidence that proposed investments are 
appropriately timed and appropriately sized for reasonably certain customer demand. Considering 
phased implementation where feasible does not delay necessary infrastructure or discourage 
economic development. Rather, it reflects prudent utility planning by aligning the pace of 
infrastructure investment with the pace of demonstrated customer demand, thereby reducing the 
potential for existing consumers to bear the costs of facilities constructed significantly in advance of 
need, or that may be excess capacity if the AI loads fail to show up as projected. 
III.  
Federal Regulatory Context 
The projects presented at this meeting arise during a period of significant evolution in federal 
transmission planning policy.  The growth in AI load interconnection requests is driving the need 
for improved local and Supplemental Project transmission planning processes that account for the 
potential cost impact of these local projects.  Although the Supplemental Projects presented through 
PJM’s M-3 process are not directly governed by the requirements of FERC Order No. 1920, the 
Commission’s recent actions reflect an increasing emphasis on transparent planning processes, 
meaningful stakeholder participation, cost-effective analyses, and well-supported planning records.   
In Order No. 1920, the Commission concluded that more forward-looking and transparent 
transmission planning is necessary to ensure that transmission investments remain just and 
reasonable over the long term.  While that rule principally addresses regional transmission planning, 
the policy objectives it advances – including transparency, robust planning assumptions, and 
meaningful stakeholder engagement—are equally relevant to customer-driven supplemental 
transmission projects.  Importantly, Order No. 890 required similar transparency, robust planning 
assumptions and meaningful stakeholder engagement in the local transmission planning process.  In

It is this cost effectiveness obligation that is missing from the current PJM Attachment M-3

Although FERC did not require changes to the local and Supplemental Project transmission

In a move toward creating greater transparency around that process, FERC recently issued show-

processes remain just and reasonable under the Federal Power Act.  OCC recognizes that  the new 
show cause proceedings do not control the disposition of the projects presented here.  However, 
these proceedings reflect FERC’s movement toward a broader regulatory focus on transparency, 
justification, cost-effectiveness and oversight of local and Supplemental Project transmission 
investments.  
 
These show cause proceedings reinforce the importance of ensuring that local and Supplemental 
transmission projects are supported by demonstrated need, prudent engineering, transparent 
planning assumptions, project cost-effectiveness and a planning record sufficient to permit 
meaningful stakeholder review before significant investments are undertaken.

IV. 
Consumer Protection Principles 
As supplemental transmission planning increasingly responds to requests from individual large-load 
customers rather than traditional reliability needs, several principles should guide the evaluation of 
proposed transmission investments.   
First, transmission projects should be supported by a clearly demonstrated need based on objective 
and transparent planning analyses. Stakeholders should have sufficient information to understand 
the assumptions underlying projected customer demand, the degree of certainty associated with 
those forecasts, and the planning criteria giving rise to the identified need.  Without this 
information, stakeholders cannot meaningfully evaluate whether proposed facilities are necessary or 
appropriately sized.  
Second, transmission investments should reflect prudent utility planning. Proposed solutions should 
be supported by reasonable engineering analyses, consideration of feasible alternatives, and where 
appropriate, opportunities for phased implementation that correspond to demonstrated customer 
commitments.  Particularly for projects involving substantial capital investment, prudent planning 
requires balancing the need to provide timely service to new consumers with the responsibility to 
avoid premature, unnecessary or potentially abandoned infrastructure investments that may 
ultimately be borne by existing consumers. 
Third, transmission investments should be developed and implemented in a manner consistent with 
longstanding regulatory principle of cost causation. Consumers should have confidence that 
investments undertaken primarily to accommodate new large-load customers are planned and 
funded in a manner that appropriately assigns costs to those AI customers, rather than shifting those 
costs to existing residential and small business consumers. 
Finally, meaningful stakeholder participation is essential to maintaining confidence in the 
transmission planning process.  The M-3 process should provide an opportunity for stakeholders to 
review proposed transmission needs and solutions before significant investment decisions are 
finalized.  That opportunity is meaningful only if stakeholders are provided sufficient information to 
understand the basis of proposed projects and if substantive stakeholder comments are thoughtfully 
considered as projects advances through the planning process. 
These principles are not intended to impede or delay needed transmission investment. Rather, they 
are intended to ensure that customer driven transmission projects are supported by transparent 
planning assumptions, prudent engineering, meaningful stakeholder review, and appropriate 
consumer protections. As transmission planning continues to evolve in response to unprecedented 
large-load growth, adherence to these principles will strengthen confidence in the M-3 process and

V. 
 Enhancing the M-3 Supplemental Project Process  
OCC appreciates PJM's efforts to improve transparency and stakeholder engagement through the 
M-3 Supplemental Project Process. As supplemental transmission planning evolves to address 
unprecedented growth in customer-driven load, there are opportunities to further strengthen the 
process while preserving the flexibility transmission owners need to respond to emerging system 
needs. 
OCC recommends that future customer-driven project presentations include additional information 
regarding the basis for projected load growth. Without disclosing confidential commercial 
information, transmission owners should identify the extent to which projected customer demand is 
supported by executed service agreements, meaningful development milestones, or other objective 
indicators demonstrating the likelihood that the projected load will materialize. Providing 
stakeholders with a better understanding of forecast certainty would improve confidence that 
proposed transmission investments are appropriately timed and sized. 
OCC encourages transmission owners to more fully discuss alternatives considered during project 
development. For projects presented at the Solutions stage, stakeholders should understand not only 
the preferred solution but also the principal alternatives evaluated, the reasons those alternatives 
were not selected, and whether phased implementation, equipment upgrades, operational changes, 
or other lower-cost options were considered. Such information would improve transparency and 
strengthen stakeholder confidence that the selected solution represents the most prudent investment. 
OCC recommends that PJM encourage transmission owners to address substantive stakeholder 
comments as projects advance through subsequent stages of the M-3 process. OCC is not suggesting 
that transmission owners be required to provide formal written responses to every comment. 
However, a brief discussion during subsequent TEAC presentations explaining whether significant 
stakeholder concerns were considered and, where appropriate, how they were addressed would 
strengthen the planning record and improve stakeholder confidence in the process. 
Finally, OCC encourages continued dialogue among PJM, transmission owners, states, consumer 
advocates, and other stakeholders regarding the evolution of supplemental transmission planning. 
Customer-driven transmission investment represents a significant and growing component of 
transmission development throughout the PJM region. As planning practices continue to evolve, 
regular stakeholder discussions regarding transparency, planning assumptions, customer

VI.  
Looking Forward 
The comments submitted herein are intended not only to address the specific supplemental 
transmission projects presented at the July 7, 2026 TEAC meeting, but also to contribute to the 
continued evolution of a transparent, well-supported, and consumer-focused supplemental 
transmission planning process. 
OCC recognizes that the electric industry is experiencing unprecedented changes driven by rapid 
load growth, technological advancement, and increasing demand for electric service from data 
centers, advanced manufacturing facilities, and other large energy users. Transmission owners and 
PJM face the significant challenge of planning for this growth while maintaining system reliability 
and providing timely service to new customers. 
At the same time, these changing conditions reinforce—not diminish—the importance of prudent 
planning, transparency, and meaningful stakeholder participation. Customer-driven supplemental 
transmission projects increasingly involve investments measured in billions of dollars and 
infrastructure that may remain in service for decades. Such investments warrant planning 
assumptions and project development processes that provide stakeholders with sufficient 
information to understand the basis for the proposed investment and evaluate whether it is 
appropriately timed, appropriately sized, and consistent with sound utility planning practices. 
The M-3 Supplemental Project Process can provide an important opportunity for stakeholders to 
contribute constructively to transmission planning before significant investment decisions are 
finalized. The effectiveness of that process, however, depends upon stakeholders receiving 
sufficient information to evaluate identified transmission needs, proposed solutions, and the 
assumptions supporting those decisions. 
The OCC supports responsible transmission investment that maintains reliability, accommodates 
appropriate economic development, and protects consumers from unnecessary costs. Increased 
transparency and continued stakeholder engagement will strengthen confidence in the supplemental 
planning process and improve the quality of transmission planning decisions for the benefit of all 
stakeholders.

transmission projects presented at the July 7, 2026 TEAC meeting. The Office recognizes the 
importance of timely transmission planning and supports investments that are necessary to maintain 
reliable electric service and accommodate responsible economic growth. 
The observations and recommendations contained in these comments are intended to support the 
objectives of the M-3 Supplemental Project Process by encouraging greater transparency, 
strengthening the planning record, and facilitating informed stakeholder participation before 
significant transmission investments advance through the planning process. 
Accordingly, OCC respectfully requests that PJM include these comments in the planning record 
for the referenced projects and encourage the applicable transmission owners to address the issues 
and requests for information raised here during the next stage of the M-3 process.  Doing so will 
enhance stakeholder confidence in the planning process and promote more informed transmission 
planning decisions. 
 
Respectfully submitted,

Request for Responses to Stakeholder Questions Regarding Ohio Supplemental Projects 
At the Needs and Solutions meeting held last month, the Office of the Ohio Consumers' Counsel ("OCC") 
submitted several questions regarding proposed Ohio supplemental transmission projects. To date, those 
questions have not been addressed. 
OCC respectfully requests that the applicable Transmission Owners provide written responses to the 
outstanding questions before these projects proceed further in the planning process. The questions concern 
matters central to evaluating the proposed projects, including the basis for the identified need, underlying 
load forecast assumptions, customer commitments, consideration of alternatives, project scope, timing, and 
expected consumer cost impacts. 
Providing responses will promote a complete and transparent planning record and facilitate meaningful 
stakeholder participation in PJM's planning process. Because the costs of supplemental transmission projects 
are ultimately borne by electricity consumers, stakeholders should have access to the information necessary 
to understand and evaluate the justification for the proposed investments. 
OCC notes that this request is separate from, and is not intended to address the merits of, any pending 
regulatory proceeding. However, the absence of responses to stakeholder questions underscores the 
importance of transparency and a well-developed record for supplemental transmission projects. Written 
responses will help ensure that stakeholders and decision-makers have information to assess whether the 
proposed projects represent prudent, cost-effective solutions to the identified system needs. 
Accordingly, OCC requests that the outstanding questions and the corresponding written responses be 
included in the planning record prior to further consideration of these projects.
